source_text: Et de patre quidem ac filio multis libris disseruerunt docti et spiritales uiri, quibus, quantum homines hominibus poterant, et quemadmodum non unus esset pater et filius, sed unum essent, et quid proprie pater esset et quid filius, insinuare conati sunt: quod ille genitor, ille genitus; ille non de filio, ille de patre; ille huius principium, unde et caput Christi dicitur, quamuis et Christus principium, sed non patris; hic uero illius imago, quamuis nulla ex parte dissimilis et omnino indifferenter aequalis. tractantur haec latius ab eis, qui non tam breuiter quam nos totius Christianae fidei professionem uolunt explicare. itaque, in quantum filius est, de patre accepit, ut sit, cum ille de filio id non acceperit: et in quantum hominem mutabilem, scilicet creaturam in melius commutandam, ineffabili misericordia temporali dispensatione suscepit, multa de illo in scripturis inueniuntur ita dicta, ut inpias haereticorum mentes prius uolentes docere quam nosse in errorem miserint, ut putarent eum non aequalem patri nec eiusdem esse substantiae, qualia sunt illa: quoniam pater maior me est, et: caput mulieris uir, caput uiri Christus, caput autem Christi deus, et: tunc et ipse subiectus erit ei, qui illi subiecit omnia, et: uado ad deum meum et deum uestrum, et nonnulla huius modi: quae omnia posita sunt, non ut naturae atque substantiae inaequalitatem significent, ne falsa sint illa: ego et pater unum sumus, et: qui me uidit, uidit et patrem meum, et: deus erat uerbum — non enim factus deus, cum omnia per ipsum facta sint — et: non rapinam arbitratus est esse aequalis deo et cetera talia, sed illa posita sunt partim propter administrationem suscepti hominis, qua dicitur: semet ipsum exinaniuit — non quia mutata est illa sapientia, cum sit omnino incommutabilis, sed quia tam humiliter hominibus innotescere uoluit — partim ergo propter hanc administrationem illa ita scripta sunt, de quibus haeretici calumniantur, partim propterea, quia filius patri debet, quod est, hoc etiam debens utique patri, quod eidem patri aequalis aut par est; pater autem nulli debet quidquid est.
thought_title: The Son's equality with the Father despite scriptural texts that seem to subordinate him
orientation: Augustine is explaining how the Son relates to the Father, and why some scriptural statements about Christ seem to make him less than the Father.
pass_a_gloss: And about the Father and the Son indeed learned and spiritual men have discoursed in many books, in which, as far as men were able to men, they have tried to suggest both how the Father and the Son are not one person, but are one thing, and what the Father properly is and what the Son is: that the former is the begetter, the latter the begotten; the former is not from the Son, the latter is from the Father; the former is the beginning of the latter, whence he is also called the head of Christ, although Christ too is a beginning, but not of the Father; the latter however is the image of the former, although in no part unlike and altogether without difference equal. These things are treated more fully by those who wish to explain the profession of the whole Christian faith not as briefly as we do. And so, in so far as he is the Son, he received from the Father that he should be, while the Father did not receive that from the Son: and in so far as he took up changeable man, that is, a creature to be changed into something better, by ineffable mercy in his earthly mission, many things are found said about him in the scriptures in such a way that they have sent the impious minds of heretics, wanting to teach before knowing, into error, so that they thought him not equal to the Father nor of the same substance, such as are those: because the Father is greater than I, and: the head of the woman is the man, the head of the man is Christ, but the head of Christ is God, and: then he himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him, and: I go to my God and your God, and some things of this kind: all of which have been set down, not to signify an inequality of nature and substance, lest those be false: I and the Father are one, and: he who has seen me has seen my Father also, and: the Word was God — for he was not made God, since all things were made through him — and: he did not think it robbery to be equal to God and other such things, but those things have been set down partly on account of the administration of the man he took up, by which it is said: he emptied himself — not because that wisdom was changed, since it is altogether unchangeable, but because he wished to become known to men so humbly — partly therefore on account of this administration those things have been written, about which heretics make false accusations, partly for this reason, because the Son owes to the Father that he is, also owing this indeed to the Father, that he is equal or on a par with the same Father; but the Father owes whatever he is to no one.

choices.why: Preserves the neuter singular 'unum' as distinct from 'unus' (one person), which Augustine explicitly contrasts
Uses the fixed glossary rendering for this key term

choices.english: administration of the man he took up
choices.why: Keeps the concrete sense of 'administratio' as the management of the assumed humanity, matching Augustine's later reference back to it
rejected: management of the man he assumed

choices.why: Captures the active slanderous sense of the verb against the heretics' misuse of scripture
Renders the comparative sense of 'par' as equal in rank or standing, distinct from 'aequalis'

pass_b_english: Learned and spiritual men have written many books about the Father and the Son, in which they have tried, as far as human beings can speak to human beings, to suggest how the Father and the Son are not one person but are one thing, and what the Father is in his own right and what the Son is. The Father is the begetter, the Son is the begotten; the Father is not from the Son, the Son is from the Father; the Father is the Son's beginning—which is why he is called the head of Christ, though Christ too is a beginning, but not of the Father—while the Son is the Father's image, though in no respect unlike him and entirely equal without any difference. Those who want to explain the whole profession of the Christian faith at greater length than we do treat these matters more fully.

So, insofar as he is the Son, he received from the Father that he exists, while the Father did not receive this from the Son. And insofar as he took up a changeable human being—a creature that was to be changed for the better—through his ineffable mercy in his earthly mission, many things are found said about him in the Scriptures in such a way that they have driven the impious minds of heretics, who wanted to teach before they learned, into error. They have made the heretics think that he is not equal to the Father and not of the same substance as him. Such statements are these: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), and “The head of the woman is the man, the head of the man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3), and “Then he himself will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him” (1 Corinthians 15:28), and “I am going to my God and your God” (John 20:17), and several others of this kind.

All of these were set down not to signify an inequality of nature and substance—otherwise these would be false: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and “Whoever has seen me has seen my Father” (John 14:9), and “The Word was God” (John 1:1)—for he was not made God, since all things were made through him—and “He did not consider equality with God something to be grasped” (Philippians 2:6), and other such statements. Rather, those statements were set down partly because of the administration of the man he took up, which is why it says: “He emptied himself” (Philippians 2:7)—not because that wisdom was changed, since it is entirely unchangeable, but because he willed to become known to human beings in such a lowly way. So partly because of this administration those things were written about which the heretics make false accusations, and partly because the Son owes to the Father that he exists, and in owing this he also owes to the Father that he is equal to or on a par with the Father. But the Father owes nothing of what he is to anyone.

problems.quote: Christ is also called the head of Christ
problems.why: English says 'head of Christ' but source says 'head of Christ' refers to the Father; the syntax is garbled.
problems.fix: which is why he is called the head of Christ

problems.quote: Christ is also a beginning, but not of the Father
problems.source_quote: quamuis et Christus principium, sed non patris
problems.why: English omits that Christ is a beginning *of something else* (creation/church), making the contrast unclear.
problems.fix: though Christ too is a beginning, but not of the Father
problems.ruling: Source 'caput Christi dicitur' = Christ called head of Christ; English 'head of Christ' is correct, but 'Christ is also a beginning' omits context.

edits.old: which is why Christ is also called the head of Christ
edits.new: which is why he is called the head of Christ

edits.old: even though Christ is also a beginning, but not of the Father
edits.new: though Christ too is a beginning, but not of the Father

fixed: Corrected 'Christ is also called the head of Christ' to 'he is called the head of Christ': source 'unde et caput Christi dicitur' refers to the Father being called the head of Christ.

Corrected 'even though Christ is also a beginning' to 'though Christ too is a beginning': source 'quamuis et Christus principium, sed non patris' uses 'et' as 'too/also', and the English should preserve the concessive force.

last_rejected.why: "Unum" here means "one" in the sense of unity/being one, not "one thing" (res). The Latin emphasizes numerical oneness of being, not a shared category.
last_rejected.ruling: Augustine's point is that Father and Son are one (unum), not one person. 'One thing' conveys this adequately.

last_rejected.quote: the Father is the Son's beginning—which is why he is called the head of Christ
last_rejected.source_quote: ille huius principium, unde et caput Christi dicitur
last_rejected.why: The Latin says "from which [beginning]" (unde) he is called head of Christ, not "which is why." The Father's being the principle/origin is the basis for the title "head of Christ."
last_rejected.fix: the Father is his beginning, from which he is also called the head of Christ
last_rejected.ruling: 'Unde' = 'from which/therefore.' 'Which is why' correctly renders the causal sense here.

last_rejected.quote: though Christ too is a beginning, but not of the Father
last_rejected.source_quote: quamuis et Christus principium, sed non patris
last_rejected.why: The Latin says Christ is "a beginning" (principium) but not "of the Father" (patris). The English "not of the Father" is ambiguous; it should clarify Christ is a beginning but not the Father's beginning.
last_rejected.fix: though Christ too is a beginning, but not the Father's
last_rejected.ruling: 'Not of the Father' correctly renders 'non patris.' The claimed ambiguity is minor, not a major error.

last_rejected.why: "Indifferenter" means "without difference/distinction" in the sense of no differentiation, not "without any difference" in the modern sense of "completely the same." The Latin emphasizes they are not distinct in nature, not that there is zero difference between persons.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Without any difference' adequately renders 'indifferenter.' The theological nuance claimed is not lost.

last_rejected.quote: through his ineffable mercy in his earthly mission
last_rejected.why: The Latin says Christ "took up" (suscepit) the human being "through ineffable mercy, in a temporal dispensation." The English makes "earthly mission" the instrument rather than the manner, and loses that Christ "took up" (assumed) the human being.
last_rejected.fix: through ineffable mercy he took up in a temporal dispensation
last_rejected.ruling: 'Earthly mission' renders 'temporali dispensatione'; 'took up' renders 'suscepit.' Both present in English.

last_rejected.quote: They have made the heretics think
last_rejected.why: The Latin purpose clause "ut putarent" depends on "ita dicta" (so spoken/written), not on a separate action by the statements. The statements were written in such a way that heretics thought... The English "They have made" introduces an active causation not in the Latin.
last_rejected.ruling: 'They have made the heretics think' conveys the result clause 'ut putarent' adequately in English.

last_rejected.why: The context shows Augustine is listing passages that affirm equality (John 10:30, John 14:9, John 1:1, Philippians 2:6). But "et cetera talia" refers back to the category of passages proving equality. The English "other such statements" is vague; these are other passages proving the same point about equality.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Other such statements' correctly renders 'et cetera talia.' Vagueness is in the Latin too.

last_rejected.quote: He did not consider equality with God something to be grasped
last_rejected.source_quote: non rapinam arbitratus est esse aequalis deo
last_rejected.why: The Latin says "he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God" (i.e., he did not regard his equality as something seized/appropriated). The English "something to be grasped" reverses the sense: the Latin says he already had equality and didn't grasp at it; the English suggests he didn't reach for something he didn't have.
last_rejected.fix: did not consider equality with God something to be seized
last_rejected.ruling: 'Something to be grasped' is a standard translation of 'rapinam' for Phil 2:6, matching the Latin.

last_rejected.quote: because of the administration of the man he took up
last_rejected.why: "Suscepti hominis" is genitive: "of the man he took up/assumed." The English "administration of the man he took up" is awkward and could mislead; better "administration connected with the man he assumed."
last_rejected.fix: because of the administration of the assumed man
last_rejected.ruling: 'Administration of the man he took up' correctly renders the genitive 'suscepti hominis.' Not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: he willed to become known to human beings in such a lowly way
last_rejected.why: "Innotescere" means "to make oneself known" or "appear," not "become known" (which suggests passive reception). The Son actively made himself known to humans.
last_rejected.fix: he willed to make himself known to human beings so humbly
last_rejected.ruling: 'Become known' is a normal rendering of 'innotescere.' Active/passive distinction is not a major error here.

last_rejected.quote: and in owing this he also owes to the Father that he is equal to or on a par with the Father
last_rejected.source_quote: hoc etiam debens utique patri, quod eidem patri aequalis aut par est
last_rejected.why: The Latin says "in also owing this certainly to the Father, that he is equal or on a par with the same Father." The English "in owing this he also owes" is garbled; the sense is that in owing his existence, he also owes his equality (as a consequence).
last_rejected.fix: in owing this too to the Father, that he is equal or on a par with that same Father
last_rejected.ruling: The English conveys that owing existence also means owing equality. Not garbled enough to mislead.

last_rejected.quote: But the Father owes nothing of what he is to anyone
last_rejected.source_quote: pater autem nulli debet quidquid est
last_rejected.why: The Latin says "the Father owes to no one whatever he is." The English "nothing of what he is" is ambiguous; it could mean "none of his attributes" rather than "nothing whatsoever of his being."
last_rejected.fix: But the Father owes what he is to no one
last_rejected.ruling: 'Nothing of what he is to anyone' correctly renders 'nulli debet quidquid est.' Not misleading.
